What felling and scraping did to the water table: a plain-language guide to the dune-restoration paper

M. Hollingham

October 2026

This companion follows the paper and adds nothing to it; where the two seem to differ, the paper is right.

It explains, without equations, the paper *Hydrological response of a coastal dune aquifer to plantation clearfell and dune scraping: a BACI analysis of a 21-year manual record* (Hollingham, 2026b). Every number in it is taken from the paper. Words in **bold** on first use are explained in the glossary at the end.

# []{#anchor}1. Why this matters

Dune slacks, the damp hollows between sand dunes, hold some of the most water-sensitive habitats in north-west Europe. What their plants need most is a shallow enough **summer minimum**, the lowest the water falls each summer, without the slack flooding all year. The typical levels of the wet-slack and dry-slack plant communities lie only about 0.4 m apart. Where the summer water table keeps falling, the slack turns to dry grassland and scrub, and the conservation interest is lost.

Two kinds of work are commonly used to win it back. One is felling conifer plantations, so that the rain the trees would have caught reaches the ground. The other is **scraping**: digging away the surface of a slack so that the ground sits closer to the water.

Both make intuitive sense, but neither is often tested against a long record. A rise in the average level is not the same as a rise in the summer low. And the weather and the coast change over the same decades as the management, so a run of wet years can flatter a failure, and a worsening background can hide a real gain.

The paper asks three questions. Did either intervention raise the water table, in which season and by how much? Why, and will the gain last? And how far do the effects of forest management reach, in particular to the eastern slacks where the stakes are highest?

# []{#anchor}2. The site and the two interventions

## []{#anchor}Where is it?

Newborough Warren lies on the south-west coast of Anglesey. Groundwater flows south from a rocky ridge through a single body of clean dune sand, then splits around a central high point. The forested western block drains south-west towards Caernarfon Bay; the open eastern dune drains towards the Menai Strait. That split matters later.

The study rests on 88 **dipwells** read by hand at the end of each month for 21 years. The wells are sorted into five groups, or **clusters**, set out in the companion aquifer paper (Hollingham, 2026a): C1 Lake Edge, C2 Dune, C3 Western Residual, C4 Main Forest and C5 Coastal Forest. The two forest clusters carry the same Corsican pine but stand on different ground: C4 on thinner sand over uneven rock, C5 on deeper coastal sand. The western shore is eroding.

## []{#anchor}The scrape

In April 2015 the ground surface of one slack, watched by the dipwell CEH36, was dug out to bring the summer water table closer to the surface. The depth dug was not surveyed; working back from how the water responded, the paper infers a lowering of about 0.43 m. CEH36 was scraped again in October 2023, when two further slacks (CEH18 and CEH21) were scraped for the first time. The unscraped slack at CEH4, and CEH22 nearer the coast, serve as the comparison wells.

## []{#anchor}The felling

In December 2017 about 4.2 ha of Corsican pine was clearfelled. The block straddles the blurred boundary between the two forest clusters, so it is not a clean single-group experiment. Only one well, WMC3, lies inside it; four sit near its edge. CEH36 lies about 340 m seaward and downhill of the felled block, which is why the two interventions have to be untangled.

# []{#anchor}3. How the comparison works

## []{#anchor}Before and after, treated and untreated

The design is called **BACI**: Before--After--Control--Impact. A treated well is compared with untreated wells, before and after the work. If the gap between them changes when the work is done, that change is the effect. Comparing gaps cancels out whatever affects treated and untreated wells alike, such as a wet year.

## []{#anchor}Five kinds of comparison well

For the felling, the wells are sorted into five **control tiers**: the felled well itself (Impact), the wells at the felled edge (Edge), unfelled forest (Forest control), wells near the coast (Coastal control), and open-dune wells further afield (Climate control).

The fairest test is against the unfelled forest, which shares the felled well's trees and ground. Comparisons against open-dune wells mix the felling up with the forest's long-standing effect and the coast, so are not read as felling effects.

## []{#anchor}Allowing for the weather

The weather before and after the felling was not the same, so the analysis carries an allowance for climate, built from a running total of rain minus evaporative demand. It also carries an allowance for the 2015 scrape, whose influence fades with distance from CEH36, so that the scrape is not mistaken for part of the felling.

## []{#anchor}Allowing for the retreating coast

The eroding shore draws the water table down near the coast, a little more each year. The felled block lies closer to the shore than the unfelled forest wells (about 550 m against 950 m), so without an allowance the coast would make the felled well look worse over time than its comparisons. A **coastal-drift allowance** absorbs this growing divergence. The amount it absorbs is consistent with the coastal effect measured across the network, and a check needing no model, comparing wells near the coast and inland, points the same way.

## []{#anchor}How sure can we be?

Monthly levels vary a great deal, and one month is close to the next, so a run of high months is less unusual than it looks; the paper allows for that. A result is called **statistically significant** when it would be unlikely to arise by chance alone; a result that is not significant may still be real, but the record cannot tell it apart from no change.

# []{#anchor}4. What felling did

## []{#anchor}A winter rise, not a summer one

Against the unfelled forest, the felled well rose by 0.128 m over October to March, a significant result. Over June to September it did not rise at all.

Averaged over the whole year, the rise was 0.108 m. That is consistent with a recovery, but on its own it is not significant once the month-to-month carry-over is allowed for. The paper treats the seasonal split as the firmer result.

The edge wells showed a small rise that was not significant. No felling response was detected outside the forest zone.

## []{#anchor}A gain that faded

The rise did not last. It came mostly in the first few years and was not sustained after 2020: split at January 2021, the step against the unfelled forest falls to a value no longer distinguishable from zero. The felled block has been kept clear by grazing, so returning trees do not explain this. The 0.108 m is the average of a front-loaded recovery.

## []{#anchor}The summer low did not move

The summer minimum showed no significant change at any tier; felled and unfelled wells moved together. A felling of this size does not relieve the summer drought. The paper resists calling the felling a success or a failure: it was followed by a winter rise, and did not do what was hoped, which is lift the summer floor.

## []{#anchor}Do the other checks agree?

Four further methods, none like-for-like with the main test, do not all point the same way, and the paper reports the disagreement rather than smoothing it over. The one direct check, using the wells inside the felled block, returns a step of similar size, though not significant on its own. Two others give a positive step at the felled well, but once the unfelled forest wells' own drift is removed (about two-thirds of the step, in one of them), neither leaves a felling-specific part that can be told apart from zero.

The step also rests on the coastal-drift allowance: without it, the felled well's step is small and not significant.

## []{#anchor}Rereading the old verdict on the forest

The plantation has long been blamed for lowering the water table. The earlier studies that said so (Betson et al., 2002) were made during the driest decade in the long rainfall record from RAF Valley, and without a design that compared treated with untreated ground and allowed for the weather. This study agrees that the canopy holds the water table down: the wells under the trees respond less to rain, and the felled well rose in winter after the felling. But the felling left the summer lows unchanged. The paper therefore reads the earlier picture as a mixture of the forest's effect and an exceptionally dry decade, whose seasonal pattern could not be untangled at the time.

## []{#anchor}Inside the model

The aquifer paper describes each well by three numbers: how far the water table rises per millimetre of rain (the **recharge sensitivity**), how far it falls per millimetre of evaporative demand (the **atmospheric draw**), and how fast it drains. Fitting them before and after the felling shows what changed. At the felled well, the draw fell (by 4.8% beyond the Climate-control wells), but the recharge sensitivity did not rise: allowing for those wells, it was 0.98 of its earlier value. That is not the pattern expected if felling had simply returned the rain the trees used to catch.

Recharge sensitivity declined at almost all wells, felled and unfelled forest alike, but hardly at all at the Climate-control wells. It is unlikely to be caused by the felling, but its independence of management is not established, and it is a candidate cause of the falling summer lows. Because it affects felled and unfelled wells alike, it cancels out in the BACI gap.

# []{#anchor}5. What scraping did

## []{#anchor}A gain where it counts

Three independent methods all find a positive effect at CEH36 in the years between the scrape and the felling. The decisive result is at the summer minimum: the scraped slack's summer low rose by 0.195 m against CEH4, a significant result and a larger, directly useful gain than the felling gave. It is a shift across more than half the gap between the typical wet-slack and dry-slack levels.

The gain persisted after the felling, even as CEH4 got drier. It is a one-off step in the ground, so the background drying carries on at the scraped slack and the gain is slowly being eroded; how often re-scraping would be needed cannot yet be read from the record. The two slacks scraped in 2023 have too short a record to show any effect.

## []{#anchor}The same mechanism as coastal erosion

Scraping does not raise the water; it lowers the ground to meet it, exactly as coastal erosion does. In both, the ground drops relative to the water table and the slope of the water table away from the lowered spot steepens. A scrape therefore acts as a local drain: it collects water flowing in sideways from the sand around it, and that inflow is what raises the slack level.

## []{#anchor}The drawdown the model predicts

If a scrape draws water in, the ground around it should lose some. The model predicts a lowering of the water table around the cut, fading with distance; the record does not show it. At WMC3, the nearest well inland, the predicted drawdown is smaller than the record can detect. So the off-site drawdown is not ruled out, but it is **modelled**, not measured. Such effects also spread through the sand over years to decades, longer than the 31 months between the first scrape and the felling.

## []{#anchor}Chasing the water inland

Suppose a scrape near the coast deepens the summer lows at wells uphill. Those wells may then look like candidates for scraping, which would push the drainage further inland, and so on. Each scrape treats the local symptom while worsening the underlying cause. The paper calls this the **chase-inland cascade**. It follows from the physics, but the record is too short to test it directly.

Summed over the whole site, the model makes the net effect of scraping a small loss of water, because the drawdown around each cut takes more than the slack gains. That loss is modelled, not observed. It does not lessen a well-sited scrape's measured local gain; it means the gain is bought, on the model, at a modest cost elsewhere.

## []{#anchor}Where to scrape

So siting matters. The coastal margin is the wrong target: there a scrape's drawdown would add to the eroding shore's. The eastern transitional slacks (the Lake Edge and Dune clusters) are a better one, where a single scrape can bring a marginal well within reach of flooding in a mildly wet winter. Any future scrape should come with a line of dipwells running uphill from it, so that any inland drawdown can be measured as it happens rather than reconstructed afterwards.

# []{#anchor}6. Forest-management scenarios

The paper also models three forest treatments from each well's three numbers:

-   **Full clearfell** gives a small gain at both forest clusters, based on the fall in draw measured at the felled well.
-   **Thinning by half** gives at most half that, because the remaining trees take up part of the water released.
-   **Broadleaf conversion**, if the leaves catch as much rain as the pines, gives a small loss: a canopy in full leaf draws more in summer than a leafless one saves in winter. If the broadleaf canopy catches less rain, the result would be a gain instead. The record cannot test either end.

The Main Forest gains more than the Coastal Forest from the same felling, because its slower drainage carries the reduced draw further. These are the low end of the range. The 4.2 ha block is narrower than the distance over which the forest's effect spreads, so any gain in rain reaching the ground there would leak into the surrounding forest. A wider felling could keep it, up to the level of open dune; with open-dune behaviour the forest clusters would stand some 0.5--0.9 m higher, whereas the felled well's recovery is about a tenth of a metre.

All three are small beside a dry-climate scenario, an order of magnitude larger. And they are worked out well by well, with no flow between wells, so they cannot show any effect at the open-dune clusters.

## []{#anchor}The Coastal Forest puzzle

The scenarios predict that felling would raise the Coastal Forest water table, yet that cluster shows the steepest decline in the network, a decline that belongs to the early record (refitted from 2011, its summer trend is flat). The paper's most plausible reading is that felling changes water lost upwards to the air, while the Coastal Forest is dominated by water drawn sideways to the retreating coast, which the scenarios do not represent. The coast accounts for about half of that cluster's summer decline, though the exact share depends on which wells the cluster contains.

# []{#anchor}7. What the plantation does to the water

## []{#anchor}Sink and shield

The paper describes the forest as both a **sink** and a **shield**. As a sink, it catches about a quarter of the rain (24%, from the one measurement made in the plantation) and draws water up through the trees. As a shield, it takes up the sun's drying energy at the canopy before it reaches the water table.

Neither role showed at the felled well as expected. Had the canopy been mainly a sink, recharge sensitivity should have risen after felling; it did not. Had it been mainly a shield, the bare ground should have dried faster; instead the draw fell.

Two readings fit the record, and it does not choose between them. Either felling worked chiefly by reducing the draw, or it did return rain to the ground but the gain spread out into the surrounding forest, because a block of about 115 m radius is narrower than the forest's reach of about 220 m. The record rules out a full local gain, but is consistent with one that has dispersed.

At the unfelled pine wells the draw rose over the same years, consistent either with the canopy maturing or with a by-product of fitting; the paper does not read it as a measured change in forest water use.

## []{#anchor}The broadleaf well

One well, NW10, sits in broadleaf woodland planted after a 1993 clearance. It responds more to rain than the pine wells, consistent with bare winter branches letting more rain through. But it is a single well in an unusual position, an indication at most.

## []{#anchor}How far does the forest's effect reach?

Not to the eastern slacks. The drainage carries any change in the forest zone south-west towards Caernarfon Bay, not east. The modelled drawdown of the existing plantation fades over about 220 m; it reaches the lake-edge wells nearest the forest at 8--72 mm and the eastern wells furthest from it at 2 mm or less. This is a modelled illustration, not a measured drawdown; the felling record agrees, finding no response outside the forest zone.

At the Lake Edge and Dune clusters, where the stakes are highest, the summer lows follow the site-wide climate signal, with no detectable influence from the forest.

# []{#anchor}8. Against the site's background

## []{#anchor}The coast and an unexplained decline

Both interventions have to be weighed against two background forces. The first is the retreating coast, which lowers the water table most at the foot of the dunes and fades inland over about 900 m. Measured as a local change in depth, it is the largest term.

The second is a decline across the whole warren that the coast does not explain. Spread over the whole site, it is the largest term when the site is taken as a whole. It is a central estimate that the record does not resolve, applied evenly by assumption although it varies across the site. Climate is the leading candidate for it, but the analysis isolates what the coast leaves behind, not a cause it has identified.

## []{#anchor}The ordering

Set against the coastal term, the modelled net loss from scraping is about 25% and the clearfell gain about 7%. Both interventions are small beside a background they cannot stop. The summer drought trajectory is approaching the wet-slack and dry-slack levels within the next one to two decades. The paper therefore frames the task at Newborough as adapting to an increasingly seasonal climate, keeping slacks able to flood, rather than restoring them to a former state.

# []{#anchor}9. What the study cannot tell

-   **Cause, with certainty.** Neither intervention was assigned at random, so features of the chosen sites may confound the result.
-   **Effects close to the felled edge.** The network was not designed to trace spreading effects, and cannot resolve a felling signal within 100 m of the felled edge.
-   **The coast's exact size.** The coast is handled by an allowance, not by modelling the delayed arrival of past retreat. Its direction is established and its rate corroborated, but its exact amount cannot be recovered from the network alone.
-   **Exact amounts in the scenarios.** Evaporative demand is worked out by a method that overestimates it in a damp maritime climate, so the scenario sizes are upper limits; their ranking does not depend on this.
-   **Flow between groups.** The scenarios are not a full flow model. Tests of how easily water moves through the sand, and a radar survey of its depth, are the priority fieldwork.
-   **Broadleaf woodland.** One well, with under four years since its canopy closed, is indicative only.
-   **The dates.** Apart from the April 2015 scrape, the intervention dates rest on the author's recollection; no operational record has been obtained.

# []{#anchor}10. The questions people will ask

## []{#anchor}Should we fell more forest?

Felling at this scale was followed by a winter rise at the felled well, but no change in the summer low, and the gain faded. A wider felling might keep a gain this one did not, but the record cannot test that. The paper concludes that the hydrological case for felling rests on objectives within the forest, not on benefits to the wider slacks.

## []{#anchor}Will felling help the eastern slacks?

The evidence says not. The forest drains towards Caernarfon Bay, not east, and no felling response was found outside the forest zone.

## []{#anchor}Is scraping safe?

It is the most directly effective intervention in the record. But it works like coastal erosion, and the model predicts it draws down the ground around it, although the record does not show this. At the coast, or repeated inland, it could chase the water inland; the eastern slacks, with dipwells uphill to watch, are the better place.

## []{#anchor}What about climate?

Climate is the leading candidate for the unexplained site-wide decline, which outweighs both interventions across the site, but the paper does not identify it as the cause.

# []{#anchor}11. Lessons for other sites

The numbers belong to Newborough; the approach travels:

1.  Judge a felling by what it delivers, which is the mean level, not the summer minimum. Quote its winter gain, and do not credit it in advance with a summer benefit. Ainsdale, on the Sefton Coast, is the closest British parallel: there too, tree cover and a drying climate act on the slack water table together (Clarke and Sanitwong Na Ayutthaya, 2010).
2.  Treat a scrape as a drain. Its length, its alignment with the slope of the water table and the level it drains to govern how it draws down the dune around it.
3.  Where a shore is retreating, expect the interior water table to fall for reasons management cannot influence, and judge interventions against that. This does not rest on Newborough alone: at Whiteford Burrows on the Gower coast, the loss of some 4% of the width of the dune spit lowered its water table by about a metre (Robins et al., 2013). What carries over between sites is the direction and the mechanism, not the rate.
4.  Put interventions and background forces on a common footing across the whole site, so that a local gain is set against its cost elsewhere. It is the ranking exercise that transfers, not the order it produced here.
5.  Commit to long baselines. A short window can mistake a passing state for a lasting result, as the fading felling gain shows.

# []{#anchor}Glossary

**Atmospheric draw.** How far the water table falls for each millimetre of evaporative demand.

**BACI (Before--After--Control--Impact).** A design comparing treated and untreated wells, before and after the work, and reading the effect from the change in the gap between them.

**Chase-inland cascade.** The risk that scraping drains the ground uphill, prompting further scrapes that push the drainage further inland.

**Cluster.** One of five groups of wells whose water rises and falls alike.

**Coastal-drift allowance.** A term in the analysis that absorbs the growing difference between wells caused by the retreating shore.

**Control tier.** A class of untreated comparison wells: unfelled forest, coastal or open dune.

**Dipwell.** A narrow perforated pipe in which the water level is measured by hand with a tape.

**Modelled.** Worked out from the model rather than seen in the record.

**Recharge sensitivity.** How far the water table rises for each millimetre of rain.

**Scraping.** Digging away the surface of a slack to bring the ground closer to the water table.

**Sink and shield.** The forest's two roles: catching rain and drawing water up (sink), and taking up drying energy at the canopy (shield).

**Statistically significant.** Unlikely to have arisen by chance alone, given how much the levels vary.

**Summer minimum.** The lowest the water table falls in a summer; the measure that decides whether a slack stays wet.
